---
title: "Methods"
description: "The seven conformal methods, grouped by whether they learn from their own mistakes, and how to pick one."
---

A **method** is one class holding the calibration math and the orchestration
around it: it takes forecasts and truths, and returns an interval. Seven ship
with `conformalforecast`, and they divide cleanly in two.

**Offline methods** calibrate once on a block of past errors and then apply a
fixed correction. They are the classical conformal guarantee, and they assume
the calibration errors and the future errors are exchangeable — that the world
does not change between the two.

**Online and adaptive methods** keep learning after calibration. Each consumes
`update(prediction, truth)` as observations arrive and moves its own knobs in
response. They exist because time series break exchangeability routinely:
regimes shift, variance drifts, a model that was well-calibrated last quarter is
not this one.

## The seven

| Method | Group | Handles | Needs |
|---|---|---|---|
| [`SplitConformal`](split) | offline | the exchangeable baseline | nothing beyond point forecasts |
| [`ConformalizedQuantileRegression`](cqr) | offline | heteroscedastic errors — noise that varies with level or season | a **quantile-capable** forecaster |
| [`WeightedSplit`](weighted_split) | offline | covariate shift — the target's features differ from the calibration set's | target features (`adapt`) or target labels (`recalibrate`) |
| [`AdaptiveConformalInference`](aci) | online | distribution shift, by moving the target `alpha` itself | a learning rate `gamma` |
| [`AggregatedAdaptiveConformalInference`](agaci) | online | shift, without having to pick `gamma` | nothing — it runs a panel of `gamma`s |
| [`NonexchangeableConformalPrediction`](nexcp) | online | shift, by down-weighting stale residuals | a decay `rho` |
| [`SequentialPredictiveConformalInference`](spci) | online | *conditional* coverage — width that varies per step | the `spci` extra (quantile-forest) |

Each method is configuration, and calibrating it returns a fitted object. The
pages below drive the **forecaster surface** —
`fitted = method.calibrate_cv(forecaster, n_windows)` then
`fitted.predict(history)` — because that is what standalone users want. The
**array surface**, `fitted = method.fit(predictions, truths)` then
`fitted.interval(predictions)`, takes no forecaster at all; see [Architecture](../concepts/architecture) for the
split and [Embedding](../concepts/embedding) for when to reach for it.

## Choosing one

Work down this list and stop at the first line that describes your problem.

1. **You have never used conformal prediction here before.** Start with
   [split conformal](split). It is one page of math, it has no knobs, and its
   coverage is a theorem rather than a hope. Everything else on this list is a
   response to a way it can fail — measure that failure before you fix it.
2. **Your errors are much larger at some times than others** — a seasonal peak,
   a high-volume series in a panel — and a constant-width band is too wide most
   of the year and too narrow at the peak. Use [CQR](cqr), if your forecaster can
   emit quantiles. Constant-width is a property of the *score*, not of conformal
   prediction.
3. **Your measured coverage drifts away from target over time.** The world moved.
   Use an online method:
   - [ACI](aci) if you are willing to tune one learning rate, and want the
     simplest thing that provably recovers long-run coverage.
   - [AgACI](agaci) if you are not — it runs several learning rates at once and
     aggregates them, which is usually what you want in production.
   - [NexCP](nexcp) if you would rather express "recent errors matter more" as a
     decay on the calibration set than as a moving target.
4. **You are predicting a different domain than you calibrated on** — a new
   region, a new customer segment, a shifted operating range — and the
   difference shows up in *features* you can measure, not in the same panel
   drifting under you over time. That is the boundary against item 3: temporal
   drift on a fixed panel is an online-method problem, a domain that differs in
   measurable ways is this one. Use [weighted split conformal](weighted_split),
   which needs either target features (`adapt(weighting=DensityRatio(...),
   target_X=...)`) or target labels (`recalibrate()`). See
   [Transfer and adaptation](../capabilities/transfer) for the full set of verbs
   and which one your data allows.
5. **Coverage is fine on average but wrong in identifiable places** — the
   interval is too wide in calm periods and too narrow in volatile ones. That is
   a conditional-coverage problem. Use [SPCI](spci), which fits a quantile
   regressor on the residual history and lets the width move with it.

Two of those choices have an **asymmetric** mode, which is a setting rather than
a different method, so it does not get its own line above. Reach for it when the
two tails do not cost the same — being short on inventory is not the mirror image
of being long on it — or when the forecaster is biased and you would rather the
band shifted than widened on both sides. [Split conformal](split) with
`symmetric=False` scores signed residuals and takes one one-sided quantile per
tail; it needs no extra capability, works through every adapter, and costs more
calibration data, since each tail now enforces its own `ceil(1 / level)` floor. [CQR](cqr) with the same flag tilts the quantile levels
it requests instead, which tracks asymmetry that varies with the input rather
than applying a constant offset — but no shipped Nixtla adapter can serve those
levels today.

::: {.callout-note}
## Coverage is not the only thing to measure

Two methods can both hit 90% and differ enormously in usefulness: the wider one
is trivially valid and tells you nothing. Compare width alongside coverage — the
Winkler score in [Diagnostics](../capabilities/diagnostics) does exactly that,
penalising width and misses on one scale.
:::

## The guarantee, and its limits

Split conformal gives finite-sample marginal coverage under exchangeability: for
any forecaster, `P(y ∈ interval) ≥ 1 - alpha`. Three qualifiers matter in
practice.

- **Marginal, not conditional.** The probability is over draws, averaged across
  series and horizons. A particular series can be systematically under-covered
  while the average is exactly right.
- **Exchangeability rarely holds for time series.** The calibration residuals
  come from the past and the test residual comes from the future; if the process
  drifts, they are not exchangeable and the guarantee degrades. The online
  methods on this page replace it with a weaker but more honest long-run
  guarantee.
- **Finite calibration sets quantise the achievable coverage.** With `n`
  calibration windows the attainable levels are multiples of `1/(n+1)`, which is
  why every method demands at least `ceil(1/alpha)` effective windows per series
  (asymmetric split and SPCI demand more) and raises
  `InsufficientCalibrationSamples` otherwise.
